Oxidising capacity is measured by the standard REDUCTION potential: the more positive \(E^{\ominus}_{red}\), the greater the tendency to be reduced, i.e. the stronger the oxidising agent.

Comparing the four values:
\[E^{\ominus}_{Sn^{4+}/Sn^{2+}} = +1.15\ V\]
\[E^{\ominus}_{Tl^{3+}/Tl} = +1.26\ V\]
\[E^{\ominus}_{Al^{3+}/Al} = -1.66\ V\]
\[E^{\ominus}_{Pb^{4+}/Pb^{2+}} = +1.67\ V\]

The largest (most positive) value is \(+1.67\ V\) for \(Pb^{4+}/Pb^{2+}\).

Chemically this is the inert-pair effect: on descending group 14 the \(+2\) state becomes progressively more stable, so \(Pb^{4+}\) is strongly oxidising, readily accepting two electrons to give \(Pb^{2+}\). Note \(Al^{3+}/Al\) with \(-1.66\ V\) is the strongest REDUCING couple, the exact opposite.

Hence option (D).

For a WEAK electrolyte the degree of dissociation \(\alpha\) is small at ordinary concentrations and rises steeply only as \(c \rightarrow 0\). Since
\[\Lambda_{m} = \alpha\,\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}\]
the molar conductivity tracks \(\alpha\).

Consequently the \(\Lambda_{m}\) vs \(\sqrt{c}\) plot for a weak electrolyte is NOT the straight line of the Debye-Huckel-Onsager equation seen for strong electrolytes. It is almost flat and low over most of the concentration range, then turns sharply upward as \(\sqrt{c}\rightarrow 0\). Read in the direction of increasing concentration, \(\Lambda_{m}\) falls very steeply at the dilute end.

Checking the options:
(A) and (B) claim only a SMALL change at infinite dilution - wrong, the change there is the steepest part of the curve, and \(\Lambda_{m}^{\circ}\) cannot even be obtained by extrapolation for this reason.
(C) has the wrong sign - dilution raises \(\Lambda_{m}\), concentration lowers it.
(D) states exactly the observed behaviour.

Hence option (D).

\[AB_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons AB_{(g)} + \tfrac{1}{2}B_{2(g)}\]
Start with 1 mol of \(AB_{2}\) and let \(x\) be the degree of dissociation.

At equilibrium: \(n_{AB_{2}} = 1-x\), \(n_{AB} = x\), \(n_{B_{2}} = x/2\), total \(= 1 + x/2\).

Since \(x \ll 1\), the total is \(\approx 1\), so the partial pressures are
\[p_{AB_{2}} \approx p,\qquad p_{AB} = xp,\qquad p_{B_{2}} = \frac{x}{2}p\]

Therefore
\[K_{p} = \frac{p_{AB}\cdot p_{B_{2}}^{1/2}}{p_{AB_{2}}} = \frac{(xp)\left(\frac{xp}{2}\right)^{1/2}}{p} = x^{3/2}\,\frac{p^{1/2}}{\sqrt{2}}\]

Solving for \(x\):
\[x^{3/2} = K_{p}\sqrt{\frac{2}{p}} \;\Rightarrow\; x^{3} = \frac{2K_{p}^{2}}{p} \;\Rightarrow\; x = \sqrt[3]{\frac{2K_{p}^{2}}{p}}\]

Hence option (C).

All four complexes have the strong-field ligand \(CN^{-}\), so all are LOW SPIN octahedral. Their stabilisation is measured by the crystal field stabilisation energy (CFSE), expressed in units of \(\Delta_{\circ}\):
\[CFSE = \left(-0.4\,n_{t_{2g}} + 0.6\,n_{e_{g}}\right)\Delta_{\circ}\]

(I) \(\left[Mn(CN)_{6}\right]^{3-}\): \(Mn^{3+}\) is \(d^{4}\), low spin \(t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{0}\)
\[CFSE = -0.4 \times 4 = -1.6\,\Delta_{\circ}\]

(II) \(\left[Co(CN)_{6}\right]^{4-}\): \(Co^{2+}\) is \(d^{7}\), low spin \(t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{1}\)
\[CFSE = -0.4 \times 6 + 0.6 \times 1 = -1.8\,\Delta_{\circ}\]

(III) \(\left[Fe(CN)_{6}\right]^{4-}\): \(Fe^{2+}\) is \(d^{6}\), low spin \(t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}\)
\[CFSE = -0.4 \times 6 = -2.4\,\Delta_{\circ}\]

(IV) \(\left[Fe(CN)_{6}\right]^{3-}\): \(Fe^{3+}\) is \(d^{5}\), low spin \(t_{2g}^{5}e_{g}^{0}\)
\[CFSE = -0.4 \times 5 = -2.0\,\Delta_{\circ}\]

Increasing magnitude of stabilisation: \(1.6 < 1.8 < 2.0 < 2.4\), i.e. \(I < II < IV < III\).

Hence option (C).

The substrate (first figure) is 1,2-dibromo-4-nitrobenzene and the reagent is sodium ethoxide in ethanol, i.e. the nucleophile \(C_{2}H_{5}O^{-}\). Aryl halides are inert to ordinary \(S_{N}1/S_{N}2\), so this must be NUCLEOPHILIC AROMATIC SUBSTITUTION, which requires a strongly electron-withdrawing group ORTHO or PARA to the leaving halogen so that the Meisenheimer intermediate's negative charge can be delocalised onto the nitro oxygens.

The \(NO_{2}\) group sits at C-4. It therefore activates C-3, C-5 (ortho) and C-1 (para).

Of the two bromines, the one at C-1 is PARA to \(NO_{2}\) and is activated; the one at C-2 is META to \(NO_{2}\) and is not.

So ethoxide displaces only the C-1 bromine:
\[1,2\text{-}(Br)_{2}\text{-}4\text{-}NO_{2}\text{-}C_{6}H_{3} + C_{2}H_{5}O^{-} \rightarrow 1\text{-}OC_{2}H_{5}\text{-}2\text{-}Br\text{-}4\text{-}NO_{2}\text{-}C_{6}H_{3}\]

Option (A) shows exactly this: ethoxy at C-1, bromine retained at C-2, nitro at C-4. Option (C) substitutes at the unactivated meta position, option (B) replaces both bromines, and option (D) replaces the nitro group instead.

Hence option (A).

For the cell \(Mg\,|\,Mg^{2+}(aq)\,\|\,Ag^{+}(aq)\,|\,Ag\):

Anode (oxidation): \(Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^{-}\)
Cathode (reduction): \(2Ag^{+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow 2Ag\)
Overall: \(Mg + 2Ag^{+} \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2Ag\), so \(n = 2\).

The reaction quotient uses the stoichiometric coefficients, and solids have unit activity:
\[Q = \frac{\left[Mg^{2+}\right]}{\left[Ag^{+}\right]^{2}}\]

The Nernst equation gives
\[E_{cell} = E_{cell}^{\circ} - \frac{RT}{2F}\ln\frac{\left[Mg^{2+}\right]}{\left[Ag^{+}\right]^{2}}\]
and inverting the logarithm's argument flips the sign:
\[E_{cell} = E_{cell}^{\circ} + \frac{RT}{2F}\ln\frac{\left[Ag^{+}\right]^{2}}{\left[Mg^{2+}\right]}\]

Two checks eliminate the distractors: \(\left[Ag^{+}\right]\) must be SQUARED (rules out A and C), and with \(\left[Ag^{+}\right]^{2}\) on top the sign must be \(+\) (rules out D).

Hence option (B).

Melting point in a transition series tracks the number of unpaired \(d\) electrons available for metallic (interatomic) bonding, peaking near the middle of each series.

Group 7 / group 8 pairs, 3d series: \(Mn\) has the exceptionally stable half-filled \(3d^{5}4s^{2}\) configuration, whose electrons are reluctant to delocalise, so \(Mn\) melts abnormally LOW.
\[Mn\ (1246^{\circ}C) < Fe\ (1538^{\circ}C)\]

4d series: the same pattern holds, \(Tc\) below \(Ru\).
\[Tc\ (2157^{\circ}C) < Ru\ (2334^{\circ}C)\]

5d series: here the order REVERSES. Rhenium has the strongest interatomic bonding of the pair and is the second-highest melting metal known after tungsten.
\[Os\ (3033^{\circ}C) < Re\ (3186^{\circ}C)\]

So \(Mn < Fe\), \(Tc < Ru\) and \(Os < Re\).

Hence option (C). Note that (B) is the trap: it gets the first two pairs right but keeps the 5d pair in the same order instead of reversing it.

The gas is heated at a fixed pressure of 1.00 atm, so the 500 J is \(q_{p} = n\,C_{p,m}\,\Delta T\).

Argon is MONATOMIC, so
\[C_{v,m} = \tfrac{3}{2}R = 1.5 \times 8.3 = 12.45\ J\,K^{-1}mol^{-1}\]
\[C_{p,m} = \tfrac{5}{2}R = 2.5 \times 8.3 = 20.75\ J\,K^{-1}mol^{-1}\]

Temperature rise:
\[\Delta T = \frac{q_{p}}{n\,C_{p,m}} = \frac{500}{0.5 \times 20.75} = \frac{500}{10.375} = 48.2\ K\]
\[T_{final} = 298 + 48.2 = 346.2\ K\]

Change in internal energy (a state function, always \(nC_{v,m}\Delta T\)):
\[\Delta U = 0.5 \times 12.45 \times 48.2 = 300\ J\]

As a check, \(\Delta U = q_{p} - p\Delta V = 500 - nR\Delta T = 500 - 0.5 \times 8.3 \times 48.2 = 500 - 200 = 300\ J\).

Hence \(346.2\ K\) and \(300\ J\), option (A). The trap in options (C) and (D) is equating \(\Delta U\) with the 500 J supplied, which is only valid at constant volume.

The rate law is set by the SLOW (rate-determining) step:
\[A + B_{2} \xrightarrow{k_{2}} AB + B \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad rate = k_{2}[A][B_{2}]\]

\(A\) is a reactive intermediate and cannot appear in the final rate law, so eliminate it using the preceding FAST pre-equilibrium:
\[A_{2} \rightleftharpoons A + A,\qquad K = \frac{k_{1}}{k_{-1}} = \frac{[A]^{2}}{[A_{2}]}\]
\[\Rightarrow [A] = \left(K[A_{2}]\right)^{1/2}\]

Substituting:
\[rate = k_{2}K^{1/2}[A_{2}]^{1/2}[B_{2}]\]

Overall order \(= \tfrac{1}{2} + 1 = 1.5\).

Hence option (A). Option (D), 2, is the trap from reading the order off the balanced overall equation instead of the mechanism.

De Broglie's justification of the Bohr postulate is that the electron wave must close on itself around the orbit, so the circumference contains a whole number of wavelengths:
\[2\pi r_{n} = n\lambda \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \lambda = \frac{2\pi r_{n}}{n}\]

For hydrogen the Bohr radius of the \(n\)th orbit is \(r_{n} = n^{2}a_{0}\). For the SECOND orbit,
\[r_{2} = 2^{2}a_{0} = 4a_{0}\]

So the circumference is \(2\pi r_{2} = 8\pi a_{0}\) and
\[\lambda = \frac{8\pi a_{0}}{n}\]

(Evaluating with \(n = 2\) gives \(\lambda = 4\pi a_{0}\), the numerical wavelength in the second orbit.)

Hence option (B). Option (C), \(4\pi a_{0}/n\), is what you get by forgetting the \(n^{2}\) in \(r_{n}\) and using \(r = 2a_{0}\).

A compound is STEAM VOLATILE when it cannot hydrogen bond to water or to its own neighbours, because its hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor are locked together in an INTRAMOLECULAR (chelated) hydrogen bond. That leaves the molecule with only weak intermolecular forces, a high vapour pressure and the ability to distil over with steam.

From the figures:
(A) ORTHO-nitrophenol - the \(-OH\) and \(-NO_{2}\) are adjacent, forming a six-membered intramolecular hydrogen bond. STEAM VOLATILE.
(B) ORTHO-nitroaniline - the \(-NH_{2}\) and \(-NO_{2}\) are adjacent and chelate in the same way. STEAM VOLATILE.
(C) PARA-aminophenol - the two groups are on opposite ends of the ring and cannot reach each other, so they hydrogen bond INTERMOLECULARLY. High melting, low volatility. NOT steam volatile.
(D) PARA-aminophenol (drawn mirrored) - same reasoning. NOT steam volatile.

Only (A) and (B) are steam volatile, which is option (C).
